title: Fame forgets
hook: everyone who remembers you will soon die too (Meditations 4.19)

segments.voice: Yesterday: time gained. Your line was time gained. Which comparison did you skip, and where did those minutes go instead? Day five hundred fifty-six.

Name your great-grandparents. All eight of them. Most people can't. These were people who worked, loved, worried about money, told jokes at dinner, and were, for a while, the center of somebody's world. Three generations later, many of their names are gone even from their own family. Marcus Aurelius, a man whose face was stamped on coins across an empire, did that same arithmetic about himself. And he didn't find it sad. He found it freeing. Today: fame forgets.
screen: `NAME ALL EIGHT GREAT-GRANDPARENTS.` → `THREE GENERATIONS LATER.` → `FAME FORGETS.`

segments.voice: First, the chain of the forgetting. In the nineteenth entry of book four Marcus writes about the person who longs to be remembered after death. They don't stop to think, he says, that every one of those who remember them will soon die too, and then those who come after, until the whole memory goes out, passed from one person to the next, through people who admire and then die. Second, suppose they don't die. Then Marcus pushes further. Suppose the people who remember you were immortal, and the memory too. What would that be to you? You'd be gone. Praise can't reach the dead. Third, even praise now. And to the living, he asks, what is praise, except for some practical use? It's information at best. It doesn't make the act better or worse. Fourth, no credit. So what's left is the act itself. If you do good to be remembered, you're building on the one thing guaranteed to dissolve. If you do it because it's good, it's complete the moment it's done. This sounds bleak only for a moment. Then it lightens. Most of us carry a quiet weight: will anyone notice, will this count, will they know it was me? Marcus sets it down. Nobody will remember, in the end. Which means you're free to do the good thing without an audience, the way your great-grandparents did most of theirs. They're forgotten. Their kindness isn't undone. It's in you, somewhere, uncredited.
screen: `EVERYONE WHO REMEMBERS WILL DIE TOO.` · `EVEN IF THEY DIDN'T, WHAT IS IT TO YOU?` · `PRAISE DOESN'T CHANGE THE ACT.` · `THE ACT IS COMPLETE WHEN DONE.` · then, large: `NO CREDIT.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of one person in your family line whose name you don't know, someone two or three generations back. Picture them at the end of an ordinary day, having done some small good nobody wrote down. Let them be uncredited and complete. Then choose one thing you could do today for no credit: something nobody will thank you for, or know was you. The bell holds the time.
Fame forgets. Marcus notes that everyone who remembers you will die too; so do good for its own sake, complete without credit. Today's word.
Your line: no credit. Do one good thing today that nobody will know was you. Day five hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes answer Meditations 4.19 with anonymous acts: a good deed done so that no one will know who did it.

original.note: Greek, 'opinion, reputation, glory': what other people think of you, the fame Marcus says forgets.

trapdoor: what you thought: fame doesn't last.
what it means: since memory fades, do good for its own sake, complete without anyone's credit.
what a scholar hears: Marcus's word here is something like 'after-fame', fame after death, a prize Roman nobles chased with statues and inscriptions.

notes: 4.19 paraphrased: he who has a vehement desire for posthumous fame does not consider that every one who remembers him will himself also die very soon, then those who succeed them, until the whole remembrance is extinguished as it is transmitted through men who foolishly admire and perish; suppose those who remember were immortal, what is it to you? And to the living, what is praise, except for some utility? Confirm.
The Greek for posthumous fame in 4.19 is often given as husterophemia; the trapdoor paraphrases it as 'after-fame'. Confirm. The original game uses the common word doxa.
Marcus's portrait on coinage across the empire: standard; confirm wording.
